claim: OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG drive the acquisition of pluripotency largely at the transcriptional level.
source: Acquisition of pluripotency is driven largely at the transcriptional level by activators OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG that must in turn cooperate with diverse coactivators to execute stem cell-specific gene expression programs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: The dyskerin (DKC1) ribonucleoprotein complex functions as an OCT4/SOX2 coactivator.
source: Using a biochemically defined in vitro transcription system that mediates OCT4/SOX2 and coactivator-dependent transcription of the Nanog gene, we report the purification and identification of the dyskerin (DKC1) ribonucleoprotein complex as an OCT4/SOX2 coactivator whose activity appears to be modulated by a subset of associated small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the identification of DKC1 complex as a coactivator through biochemical purification and in vitro transcription assays.

claim: The DKC1 complex coactivator activity is modulated by a subset of associated small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs).
source: Using a biochemically defined in vitro transcription system that mediates OCT4/SOX2 and coactivator-dependent transcription of the Nanog gene, we report the purification and identification of the dyskerin (DKC1) ribonucleoprotein complex as an OCT4/SOX2 coactivator whose activity appears to be modulated by a subset of associated small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs).
evidence: The abstract states that snoRNAs modulate DKC1 coactivator activity based on experimental observations.

claim: The DKC1 complex occupies enhancers of key pluripotency genes in embryonic stem cells.
source: The DKC1 complex occupies enhancers and regulates the expression of key pluripotency genes critical for self-renewal in embryonic stem (ES) cells.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by ChIP data shown in the results.

claim: The DKC1 complex regulates the expression of key pluripotency genes critical for self-renewal in ES cells.
source: The DKC1 complex occupies enhancers and regulates the expression of key pluripotency genes critical for self-renewal in embryonic stem (ES) cells.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by gene expression analysis after DKC1 knockdown.

claim: Depletion of DKC1 in fibroblasts significantly decreased the efficiency of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell generation.
source: Depletion of DKC1 in fibroblasts significantly decreased the efficiency of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell generation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by reprogramming experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The DKC1 complex has an unanticipated transcriptional role in stem cell maintenance and somatic cell reprogramming.
source: This study thus reveals an unanticipated transcriptional role of the DKC1 complex in stem cell maintenance and somatic cell reprogramming.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement summarizing the novel findings of the study.

claim: OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG control the acquisition of pluripotency in the epiblast during early embryogenesis.
source: The acquisition of pluripotency in the epiblast, a transient population of cells with unrestricted developmental potential during early embryogenesis, is controlled by a core set of transcription factors that include OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG (Nichols et al., 1998; Avilion et al., 2003; Chambers et al., 2003; Mitsui et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The undifferentiated stem state can be captured as embryonic stem (ES) cells.
source: This undifferentiated, pristine stem state can be captured as embryonic stem (ES) cells (Evans and Kaufman, 1981; Martin, 1981; Brook and Gardner, 1997), regenerated from somatic cells by cell fusion and nuclear transfer (Yamanaka and Blau, 2010), or by the ectopic expression of defined transcription factors (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Yu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational ES cell literature.

claim: Pluripotency can be regenerated from somatic cells by cell fusion and nuclear transfer.
source: This undifferentiated, pristine stem state can be captured as embryonic stem (ES) cells (Evans and Kaufman, 1981; Martin, 1981; Brook and Gardner, 1997), regenerated from somatic cells by cell fusion and nuclear transfer (Yamanaka and Blau, 2010), or by the ectopic expression of defined transcription factors (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Yu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamanaka and Blau, 2010.

claim: Pluripotency can be regenerated by ectopic expression of defined transcription factors.
source: This undifferentiated, pristine stem state can be captured as embryonic stem (ES) cells (Evans and Kaufman, 1981; Martin, 1981; Brook and Gardner, 1997), regenerated from somatic cells by cell fusion and nuclear transfer (Yamanaka and Blau, 2010), or by the ectopic expression of defined transcription factors (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Yu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Yu et al., 2007.

claim: Reprogrammed pluripotent cells display a transcriptome highly similar to ES cells.
source: These reprogrammed pluripotent cells display a transcriptome that is highly similar to ES cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG play key roles in the maintenance of pluripotency in ES cells.
source: Not surprisingly, OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG also play key roles in the maintenance of pluripotency in ES cells and its reacquisition in induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells by targeting a common set of genes that underpin the pluripotent state (Boyer et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2008.

claim: OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG play key roles in the reacquisition of pluripotency in iPS cells.
source: Not surprisingly, OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG also play key roles in the maintenance of pluripotency in ES cells and its reacquisition in induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells by targeting a common set of genes that underpin the pluripotent state (Boyer et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2008.

claim: Stem cell-specific gene expression programs require a growing list of co-regulators including enhancer binding transcription factors, coactivators, chromatin remodelers, and histone modifiers.
source: However, execution of these complex stem cell-specific gene expression programs also require a growing list of co-regulators including enhancer binding transcription factors (KLF4 (Jiang et al., 2008), SALL4 (Wu et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2006), ESRRB (Zhang et al., 2008; Festuccia et al., 2012)), coactivators (Mediator (Chia et al., 2010; Kagey et al., 2010), YAP (Lian et al., 2010), TAFs/TFIID (Fong et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2011; Pijnappel et al., 2013)), chromatin remodelers (esBAF (Ho et al., 2009)), and histone modifiers (p300/CBP (Chen et al., 2008), the trithorax histone methyltransferase (Ang et al., 2011)).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The XPC DNA repair complex functions as a transcriptional coactivator in ES cells.
source: Intriguingly, recent studies have implicated additional cofactors that have not been traditionally associated with transcriptional regulation, such as the XPC DNA repair complex (Fong et al., 2011), as well as microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs as part of the pluripotency regulatory network (Wilusz et al., 2009; Orkin and Hochedlinger, 2011; Jia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fong et al., 2011.

claim: MicroRNAs and long non-coding RNAs are part of the pluripotency regulatory network.
source: Intriguingly, recent studies have implicated additional cofactors that have not been traditionally associated with transcriptional regulation, such as the XPC DNA repair complex (Fong et al., 2011), as well as microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs as part of the pluripotency regulatory network (Wilusz et al., 2009; Orkin and Hochedlinger, 2011; Jia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wilusz et al., 2009; Orkin and Hochedlinger, 2011; Jia et al., 2013.

claim: The XPC complex safeguards genome integrity by scanning the genome for DNA damage and initiating excision repair.
source: For example, the XPC complex safeguards genome integrity of self-renewing stem cells as well as their differentiated progeny by scanning the genome for DNA damage and initiating excision repair (de Laat et al., 1999; Riedl et al., 2003; Sugasawa, 2011), while YAP controls the expansion of stem cells by sensing diffusible signals and external cues in the niche (Lian et al., 2010; Dupont et al., 2011; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Laat et al., 1999; Riedl et al., 2003; Sugasawa, 2011.

claim: YAP controls the expansion of stem cells by sensing diffusible signals and external cues in the niche.
source: For example, the XPC complex safeguards genome integrity of self-renewing stem cells as well as their differentiated progeny by scanning the genome for DNA damage and initiating excision repair (de Laat et al., 1999; Riedl et al., 2003; Sugasawa, 2011), while YAP controls the expansion of stem cells by sensing diffusible signals and external cues in the niche (Lian et al., 2010; Dupont et al., 2011; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lian et al., 2010; Dupont et al., 2011; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2014.

claim: The XPC complex and YAP are highly enriched in ES and iPS cells.
source: Indeed, coactivators like the XPC complex and YAP are highly enriched in ES and iPS cells perhaps because they are performing double duty (Ramalho-Santos et al., 2002; Lian et al., 2010; Fong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramalho-Santos et al., 2002; Lian et al., 2010; Fong et al., 2011.

claim: Depletion of the XPC complex and YAP compromises pluripotency gene expression, stem cell maintenance, and somatic cell reprogramming.
source: Not surprisingly, depletion of these multifaceted complexes compromises pluripotency gene expression, stem cell maintenance, and somatic cell reprogramming (Lian et al., 2010; Fong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lian et al., 2010; Fong et al., 2011.

claim: Only a small fraction (0.1–1%) of somatic cells become iPS cells during reprogramming.
source: Somatic cell reprogramming by a small cadre of specific transcription factors is thought to be a stochastic and inefficient process where only a small fraction (0.1–1%) of somatic cells become iPS cells (Buganim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buganim et al., 2013.

claim: The induction of reprogramming-permissive somatic cells may depend on cell-intrinsic determinants.
source: However, recent data suggests that the induction of these rare, reprogramming-permissive somatic cells is not entirely a random event but may depend in part on cell-intrinsic determinants that are somehow restricted to a privileged few (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claim: Privileged somatic cells exhibit ultrafast cell duplication and express higher levels of proteins involved in DNA repair, RNA processing, and cell cycle control.
source: These privileged somatic cells exhibit ultrafast cell duplication and express higher levels of proteins involved in DNA repair, RNA processing and cell cycle control (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claim: Q0.3 activity is required for the XPC coactivator complex to stimulate full, synergistic activation of the human Nanog proximal promoter by OCT4 and SOX2.
source: We previously have shown an activity present in a partially purified protein fraction, Q0.3, that is required for the XPC coactivator complex to stimulate a full, synergistic activation of the human Nanog proximal promoter by OCT4 and SOX2 but is dispensable for basal or Sp1-activated transcription (Rodda et al., 2005; Fong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rodda et al., 2005; Fong et al., 2011.

claim: Q0.3 separated from the XPC complex at the Poros-HQ anion exchange chromatographic step.
source: Q0.3 separated from the XPC complex at the Poros-HQ anion exchange chromatographic step (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A,B showing the chromatography scheme and transcription assay results.

claim: Q0.3 appeared to migrate as a single activity on a size exclusion column with an apparent molecular mass of ∼500 kDa.
source: Although Q0.3 appeared to migrate as a single activity on a size exclusion column with an apparent molecular mass (Mr) of ∼500 kDa (Figure 1C), this coactivator activity splits again into two distinct chromatographic fractions on a Poros-Heparin (Poros-HE) cation exchanger.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing the Superose 6 fractionation results.

claim: Q0.3 coactivator activity splits into two distinct chromatographic fractions (SCC-A and SCC-B) on a Poros-Heparin cation exchanger.
source: Although Q0.3 appeared to migrate as a single activity on a size exclusion column with an apparent molecular mass (Mr) of ∼500 kDa (Figure 1C), this coactivator activity splits again into two distinct chromatographic fractions on a Poros-Heparin (Poros-HE) cation exchanger. One cofactor (SCC-B) eluted at ∼0.4 M KCl whereas the second activity (SCC-A) eluted at ∼0.6 M KCl (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D showing the Poros-HE fractionation results.

claim: At least three distinct stem cell coactivators (XPC complex, SCC-A, and SCC-B) are required to generate a full, OCT4/SOX2-dependent transcriptional response.
source: Taken together, it appears that at least three distinct stem cell coactivators (one being the XPC complex) are required to generate a full, OCT4/SOX2-dependent transcriptional response.
evidence: This is inferred from the chromatographic separation and transcription assay results.

claim: SCC-A was purified from NT2 nuclear extracts with >30,000-fold increase in specific activity over six successive chromatographic columns.
source: Starting with nuclear extracts prepared from 400 L of a pluripotent embryonal carcinoma (EC) cell line NTERA-2 (NT2), we used the reconstituted transcription system supplemented with recombinant XPC complex, purified OCT4, SOX2, and a modified human Nanog template, to purify SCC-A over six successive chromatographic columns resulting in >30,000-fold increase in specific activity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and the purification scheme is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Silver staining of peak Poros-HE purified fractions revealed four major polypeptides that consistently co-purified with SCC-A activity.
source: Silver staining of the peak Poros-HE purified fractions revealed a distinct pattern of four major polypeptides that consistently co-purified with SCC-A activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified SCC-A as the dyskerin (DKC1) complex comprised of DKC1, GAR1, NHP2, and NOP10 subunits.
source: Tryptic digestion of the four excised gel bands followed by mass spectrometry analysis revealed SCC-A to be the dyskerin (DKC1) complex comprised of DKC1, GAR1, NHP2, and NOP10 subunits (Figure 2A) (Meier, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the text and the protein identities are shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Core subunits of the DKC1 and XPC complexes were highly enriched in the P1M phosphocellulose fraction compared to total nuclear extract.
source: Consistent with our previous observation that the bulk of OCT4/SOX2 coactivator activity resides in the 1 M KCl fraction (P1M) (Fong et al., 2011), core subunits of the DKC1 and XPC complexes (and SCC-B, data not shown) were highly enriched in P1M compared to total nuclear extract or the transcriptionally inactive 0.3 and 0.5 M fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The DKC1 complex is an evolutionarily conserved, four-subunit protein complex that interacts with H/ACA small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs).
source: The DKC1 complex is an evolutionarily conserved, four-subunit protein complex that interacts with a large heterogeneous class of small non-coding RNAs called H/ACA small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) (Meier, 2005; Terns and Terns, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meier, 2005; Terns and Terns, 2006.

claim: The assembly of a DKC1 RNP in vivo follows a multi-step process mediated by the protein chaperones SHQ1 and NAF1.
source: The assembly of a DKC1 RNP in vivo follows an elaborate, multi-step process mediated by the protein chaperones SHQ1 and NAF1 (Darzacq et al., 2006; Grozdanov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Darzacq et al., 2006; Grozdanov et al., 2009.

claim: GAR1 replaces NAF1 in the intermediate DKC1 complex to form the mature RNP after snoRNAs are incorporated and properly processed.
source: The GAR1 subunit subsequently replaces NAF1 in the intermediate complex containing NAF1, DKC1, NHP2, and NOP10 to form the mature RNP only after snoRNAs are incorporated and properly processed (Kiss et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kiss et al., 2010.

claim: H/ACA snoRNAs guide sequence-specific pseudouridylation of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) and spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) by the catalytic subunit DKC1.
source: These H/ACA snoRNAs guide sequence-specific pseudouridylation of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) and spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) by the catalytic subunit DKC1 (Liang and Li, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liang and Li, 2011.

claim: The DKC1 complex plays a key role in the biogenesis of telomerase by binding and promoting the processing and intranuclear trafficking of telomerase RNA (TERC).
source: The DKC1 complex also plays a key role in the biogenesis of telomerase by binding and promoting the processing and intranuclear trafficking of telomerase RNA (TERC) (Egan and Collins, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Egan and Collins, 2012.

claim: An RNA-free, ternary 'apo-complex' of DKC1 can be generated in vitro.
source: Given the intimate association of the DKC1 complex with numerous RNAs and the multiple factors required to assemble the RNP in vivo, it is remarkable that an RNA-free, ternary 'apo-complex' can be generated in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a notable finding in the context of the study.

claim: Crystal structures of archeal and yeast partial and holo-complexes of DKC1 revealed direct protein–protein contacts among the four subunits independent of RNA.
source: Indeed, several crystal structures of the archeal and yeast partial and holo-complexes of DKC1 revealed direct protein–protein contacts among the four subunits independent of RNA (Li and Ye, 2006; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Ye, 2006; Li et al., 2011.

claim: Recombinant human DKC1 complex was purified from Sf9 cells to near homogeneity.
source: Using a combination of conventional chromatography and affinity purification procedures, we were able to efficiently purify the recombinant DKC1 complex from Sf9 cells to near homogeneity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A significant amount of Sf9 RNAs co-purified with the human DKC1 complex expressed in Sf9 cells.
source: It is important to point out that a significant amount of Sf9 RNAs co-purified with the human DKC1 complex as determined by 5′ end radiolabeling of the purified RNA species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The biogenesis pathway and machinery for DKC1 RNP assembly are at least partly conserved between human and Sf9 cells.
source: This suggests that the biogenesis pathway and machinery for DKC1 RNP assembly are at least partly conserved between human and Sf9 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sf9 RNAs co-purify with human DKC1 complex.

claim: The holo-DKC1 complex isolated from E. coli showed similar subunit stoichiometry compared to DKC1 complexes purified from NT2 cells.
source: Nonetheless, the holo-DKC1 complex isolated from E. coli showed similar subunit stoichiometry compared to DKC1 complexes purified from NT2 cells (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: The holo-DKC1 complex purified from E. coli did not contain detectable amounts of any associated RNAs.
source: More importantly, it did not appear to contain detectable amounts of any associated RNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All partial and complete recombinant DKC1 complexes exhibited similar specific activities for coactivation.
source: Remarkably, all partial and complete recombinant complexes whether produced in E. coli or Sf9 cells exhibited similar specific activities for coactivation, but were reproducibly less active than the purified native endogenous DKC1 complex from NT2 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Recombinant DKC1 complexes were reproducibly less active than the purified native endogenous DKC1 complex from NT2 cells.
source: Remarkably, all partial and complete recombinant complexes whether produced in E. coli or Sf9 cells exhibited similar specific activities for coactivation, but were reproducibly less active than the purified native endogenous DKC1 complex from NT2 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The largest subunit DKC1 and the smallest protein NOP10 are sufficient to provide the bulk of the transcriptional coactivator function.
source: Indeed, it appears that the largest subunit DKC1 and the smallest protein NOP10 are sufficient to provide the bulk of the transcriptional coactivator function and that an RNA component may not be strictly required for this moonlighting activity of the DKC1 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the DKC1-NOP10 heterodimer is active in transcription assays.

claim: An RNA component may not be strictly required for the transcriptional coactivator function of the DKC1 complex.
source: Indeed, it appears that the largest subunit DKC1 and the smallest protein NOP10 are sufficient to provide the bulk of the transcriptional coactivator function and that an RNA component may not be strictly required for this moonlighting activity of the DKC1 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the activity of recombinant RNA-free DKC1 complexes.

claim: Some mammalian snoRNAs may play a role in enhancing the transcriptional activity of the DKC1 complex.
source: Although snoRNAs may not be essential for conferring coactivator competence to the recombinant DKC1 complexes, we note that the endogenous DKC1 complexes are twofold to threefold more active than their recombinant counterparts, suggesting that some mammalian snoRNAs may play a role in enhancing the transcriptional activity of the DKC1 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher activity of endogenous DKC1 complexes compared to recombinant ones.

claim: More than 100 known H/ACA snoRNAs form an equally large number of distinct RNPs by associating with the same four core protein subunits in mammalian cells.
source: The DKC1 RNPs in mammalian cells are highly heterogeneous—with more than 100 known H/ACA snoRNAs that form an equally large number of distinct RNPs by associating with the same four core protein subunits, some of which with unknown functions (i.e. orphan snoRNAs that lack base complementarity to rRNAs or snRNAs) (Kiss et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kiss et al., 2010.

claim: Many snoRNAs are differentially expressed during neural differentiation of mouse ES cells in vitro.
source: Indeed, many snoRNAs are differentially expressed during neural differentiation of mouse ES cells in vitro (Skreka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skreka et al., 2012.

claim: As much as 60% of snoRNAs can be processed into microRNAs (miRNAs).
source: Furthermore, as much as 60% of snoRNAs can be processed into microRNAs (miRNAs), most of which have unknown targets (Ender et al., 2008; Taft et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ender et al., 2008; Taft et al., 2009.

claim: DKC1 RNPs were found to elute in a broad profile from 0.3 to 0.9 M KCl on a Poros-HQ anion exchange column with the majority eluting at ∼ 0.5 M.
source: As expected, DKC1 RNPs were found to elute in a broad profile from 0.3 to 0.9 M KCl with the majority of the complexes eluting at ∼ 0.5 M (Figure 3B), consistent with extensive heterogeneity of the DKC1 RNPs in NT2 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The various affinity-purified DKC1 RNP pools all contain stoichiometric amounts of the four core protein subunits indicating that they are likely mature RNPs.
source: The various affinity-purified DKC1 RNP pools all contain stoichiometric amounts of the four core protein subunits indicating that they are likely mature RNPs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 5′ end radiolabeling of the purified RNA species from the various affinity-purified DKC1 RNP preparations revealed distinct patterns of associated RNAs.
source: Indeed, 5′ end radiolabeling of the purified RNA species from the various affinity-purified DKC1 RNP preparations revealed distinct patterns of associated RNAs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DKC1 RNPs purified from high salt eluted fractions were enriched for longer RNAs (>180 nucleotides) and some select shorter RNAs (<100 nucleotides).
source: The DKC1 RNPs purified from high salt eluted fractions (# 22, 26, and 30) were enriched for longer RNAs (>180 nucleotides) and some select shorter RNAs (<100 nucleotides).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of Figure 3D.

claim: DKC1 RNPs purified from higher salt eluted Poros-HQ fractions displayed significantly higher specific activity than those from lower salt fractions.
source: Remarkably, DKC1 RNPs purified from higher salt eluted Poros-HQ fractions (fractions 26 and 30) displayed significantly higher specific activity than those from lower salt fractions (fractions 9 and 14) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a ∼sixfold enhancement in the specific activities of DKC1 RNPs purified from fraction 30 compared to fraction 9.
source: We estimated a ∼sixfold enhancement in the specific activities of DKC1 RNPs purified from fraction 30 compared to fraction 9, which, as we had shown in Figure 3D, contained no detectable RNAs (Figure 3E, compare lanes 3 and 13).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of Figure 3E.

claim: The bacterial apo-complex is less active than DKC1 RNPs purified from NT2 cells in supporting transcription.
source: However, the fact that this apo-complex activated transcription with reduced specific activity (Figure 3E, compare lanes 1 and 3) is consistent with our previous observation that the bacterial apo-complex is less active than DKC1 RNPs purified from NT2 cells in supporting transcription (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figures 2D and 3E.

claim: Recombinant DKC1 RNPs purified from Sf9 cells exhibited low specific activities similar to the bacterial and apo-complexes despite containing insect snoRNAs.
source: Paradoxically, recombinant DKC1 RNPs purified from Sf9 cells contained insect snoRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but exhibited low specific activities similar to the bacterial and apo-complexes suggesting that some RNAs may be inhibitory.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figures 2D and 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A subset of mammalian non-coding snoRNAs may enhance the DKC1 coactivator function while other RNAs may inhibit its transcription activity.
source: Taken together, these results uncover a previously unrecognized gene regulatory role of the DKC1 RNP complex wherein a subset of mammalian non-coding snoRNAs may enhance the DKC1 coactivator function while other RNAs may inhibit its transcription activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential activities of DKC1 RNPs with different associated RNAs.

claim: Addition of individual coactivator complexes (DKC1, XPC, or SCC-B) only marginally activated Nanog transcription.
source: Addition of individual coactivator complexes only marginally activated Nanog transcription (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When the DKC1 complex was supplemented with the XPC complex, there was a noticeable increase in transcriptional output that was substantially further enhanced by adding SCC-B.
source: However, when the DKC1 complex was supplemented with the XPC complex, we observed a noticeable increase in transcriptional output that was substantially further enhanced by adding the third coactivator, SCC-B (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The DKC1, XPC, and SCC-B coactivators are co-dependent in supporting an optimal, synergistic activation of the Nanog gene by OCT4 and SOX2.
source: These results confirmed the co-dependent nature of these three coactivators in supporting an optimal, synergistic activation of the Nanog gene by OCT4 and SOX2.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcription assay results in Figure 4A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of the XPC complex pulled down the DKC1 complex both in the presence and absence of OCT4 and SOX2.
source: Immunoprecipitation of the XPC complex pulled down the DKC1 complex both in the presence and absence of the activators.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: The DKC1 complex may function as an OCT4/SOX2 coactivator in part through a direct physical interaction with the XPC complex.
source: This finding suggests that the DKC1 complex may function as an OCT4/SOX2 coactivator in part through a direct physical interaction with the XPC complex, which in turn binds OCT4 and SOX2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: WDR79, a known accessory protein of the mature DKC1 RNP, was identified as a candidate XPC-interacting protein in a global proteomic study.
source: In support of this observation, a recent global proteomic study using large scale biochemical fractionation of human cell extracts to isolate stable protein complexes identified WDR79, a known accessory protein of the mature DKC1 RNP (Tycowski et al., 2009; Jady et al., 2012), as a candidate XPC-interacting protein (Havugimana et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tycowski et al., 2009; Jady et al., 2012; Havugimana et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations in the Dkc1, Nhp2, and Nop10 genes have been linked to dyskeratosis congenita (DC).
source: Mutations in the Dkc1, Nhp2, and Nop10 genes have been linked to dyskeratosis congenita (DC), a rare but fatal human genetic disorder that impairs stem cell function and proliferation generally attributed to defects in telomerase or ribosome biogenesis (Mitchell et al., 1999; Mason and Bessler, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 1999; Mason and Bessler, 2011.

claim: All mutant DKC1 RNPs (D125A, A353V, L37del, Δ22C, and R34W) were consistently more active than the WT holo-complex in potentiating OCT4/SOX2-mediated transcription.
source: Remarkably, all mutant DKC1 RNPs, whether they were mock or nuclease-treated to partially remove the associated Sf9 small RNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), were consistently more active than the WT holo-complex in potentiating OCT4/SOX2-mediated transcription (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neither the enzymatic activity nor amino acids mutated in DC are essential for DKC1 coactivator activity.
source: Therefore, it appeared that neither the enzymatic activity nor amino acids mutated in DC are essential for coactivator activity although the enhanced coactivator phenotype could lead to changes in gene expression and altered stem cell function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DC mutants are more active than wild-type.

claim: Efficient crosslinking of DKC1 to the Oct4 enhancer by formaldehyde requires pre-treatment of ES cells with a protein–protein cross-linker (EGS).
source: We found that efficient crosslinking of DKC1 to the Oct4 enhancer by formaldehyde requires the pre-treatment of ES cells with a protein–protein cross-linker (ethylene glycol bis[succinimidylsuccinate] or EGS) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sites of DKC1 occupancy at the Oct4, Nanog, Sox2 genes coincide with those of OCT4 and SOX2 binding to enhancer and promoter DNA sequences in mouse ES cell line D3.
source: ChIP-qPCR analysis revealed that sites of DKC1 occupancy at the Oct4, Nanog, Sox2 genes indeed coincide with those of OCT4 (Boyer et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2006) and SOX2 binding to enhancer and promoter DNA sequences (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) in the mouse ES cell line D3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: DKC1 binding is enriched at the enhancers of Oct4 and Nanog in human ES cell line H9.
source: Importantly, DKC1 binding is also enriched at the enhancers of Oct4 and Nanog in human ES cell line H9 (Figure 5B) and EC cell line NT2 (Figure 5C), thus confirming the generality of a co-recruitment mechanism to transcriptional regulatory elements in pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DKC1 binding is enriched at the Oct4 promoter in human EC cell line NT2.
source: Importantly, DKC1 binding is also enriched at the enhancers of Oct4 and Nanog in human ES cell line H9 (Figure 5B) and EC cell line NT2 (Figure 5C), thus confirming the generality of a co-recruitment mechanism to transcriptional regulatory elements in pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DKC1 was not significantly enriched at the Fgf4 gene in D3 cells.
source: Curiously, we failed to detect a significant enrichment of DKC1 at some OCT4/SOX2-target genes such as Fgf4 in D3 cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The DKC1 complex may be differentially employed by OCT4 and SOX2 to regulate a subset of their target genes.
source: This suggests that the DKC1 complex may be differentially employed by OCT4 and SOX2 to regulate a subset of their target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DKC1 is not enriched at all OCT4/SOX2 target genes.

claim: Over 90% of snoRNAs are embedded in the introns of coding and non-coding genes.
source: Since over 90% of snoRNAs are embedded in the introns of coding and non-coding genes (Filipowicz and Pogacic, 2002), the DKC1 complex has also been found to localize at gene bodies where it is thought to co-transcriptionally process nascent snoRNAs (Darzacq et al., 2002; Ballarino et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Filipowicz and Pogacic, 2002; Darzacq et al., 2002; Ballarino et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2005.

claim: The DKC1 complex co-occupying pluripotent gene promoters and enhancer elements with OCT4 and SOX2 in ES cells suggests a classical coactivator function rather than acting purely as a snoRNP maturation factor.
source: Now our finding of the DKC1 complex co-occupying pluripotent gene promoters and enhancer elements with sequence-specific activators OCT4 and SOX2 in ES cells strongly suggests a classical coactivator function of the DKC1 complex rather than acting purely as a snoRNP maturation factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing DKC1 occupancy at enhancers and promoters.

claim: The DKC1, GAR1, and NOP10 subunits are highly enriched in pluripotent D3 cells.
source: Consistent with the notion that the DKC1 complex is performing as a stem cell-specific coactivator in ES cells, the DKC1, GAR1, and NOP10 subunits are highly enriched in pluripotent D3 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The levels of DKC1, GAR1, and NOP10 in ES cells decreased rapidly upon retinoic acid (RA)-induced differentiation.
source: Their levels in ES cells decreased rapidly upon retinoic acid (RA)-induced differentiation while general transcription factor TFIIB and loading control β-Actin remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on western blot analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: Components of the C/D snoRNP (FBL and NOP58) stayed largely constant during RA-induced differentiation of ES cells.
source: Importantly, the selective decrease of DKC1 levels was not simply a reflection of a reduced proliferative state or protein translational activity in differentiating ES cells because components of the C/D snoRNP (FBL and NOP58), another major machinery involved in the ribosome biogenesis pathway, stayed largely constant (Su et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by western blot data in Figure 6A and citation to Su et al., 2013.

claim: Transcription of the Dkc1 gene is regulated by OCT4 and NANOG in ES and iPS cells.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that transcription of the Dkc1 gene is regulated by OCT4 and NANOG in ES and iPS cells (Agarwal et al., 2010), thus providing a transcriptional mechanism whereby Dkc1 expression levels are tightly coupled to the pluripotent state.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2010.

claim: Knockdown of DKC1 but not XPC resulted in co-depletion of the small NOP10 subunit.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of DKC1 but not XPC resulted in co-depletion of the small NOP10 subunit indicating that the stability of individual subunits likely depends on the integrity of the DKC1 complex (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: shRNA-mediated silencing of XPC or DKC1 resulted in pronounced morphological abnormalities including rapid collapse of ES cell colonies and appearance of large, flattened cells with concurrent dramatic reductions in alkaline phosphatase activity.
source: Compared to control knockdown D3 cells, shRNA-mediated silencing of XPC (shXPC) or DKC1 (shDKC1-1 and shDKC1-2) resulted in pronounced morphological abnormalities including rapid collapse of the tightly packed ES cell colonies and appearance of large, flattened cells with concurrent dramatic reductions in alkaline phosphatase activity, all indicative of enhanced spontaneous differentiation of ES cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mouse ES cells lacking telomerase activity (Terc −/−) can be maintained in culture for over 300 population doublings with no observable impact on growth rate and only a very mild effect on ribosome biogenesis.
source: However, mouse ES cells lacking telomerase activity (Terc −/− (Niida et al., 1998)) or carrying a pathogenic mutation in Dkc1 (A353V (Mochizuki et al., 2004)) can be maintained in culture for over 300 population doublings with no observable impact on growth rate and only a very mild effect on ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Niida et al., 1998; Mochizuki et al., 2004.

claim: Single knockdown of XPC or DKC1 in D3 cells resulted in a significant reduction in mRNA levels of core pluripotency genes including Nanog, Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and Fgf4.
source: Consistent with the evident morphological changes associated with compromised stem cell identity, single knockdown of XPC or DKC1 in D3 cells resulted in a significant reduction in mRNA levels of core pluripotency genes including Nanog, Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, as well as stem cell marker Fgf4 (Figure 6D), while housekeeping gene Gapdh remain stable (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of XPC and DKC1 did not further reduce the expression of pluripotency genes compared to single knockdowns.
source: Interestingly, simultaneous knockdown of XPC and DKC1 did not further reduce their expression.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on qPCR analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: Depletion of DKC1 or XPC upregulated the expression of neuroectodermal marker Fgf5 and trophoblast-specifier Cdx2 at the expense of Gata6, while mesodermal marker T remained unchanged.
source: Depletion of DKC1 or XPC upregulated the expression of neuroectodermal maker Fgf5 and trophoblast-specifier Cdx2 at the expense of Gata6, a primitive endoderm marker, while mesodermal marker T remained unchanged (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Double knockdown of DKC1 and XPC appeared to further augment the expression of Cdx2 but not Fgf5.
source: Double knockdown of DKC1 and XPC appeared to further augment the expression of Cdx2 but not Fgf5.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on qPCR analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: The observed differentiation bias in DKC1 and XPC knockdown ES cells may be in part due to the reduced levels of OCT4 and NANOG.
source: The observed differentiation bias in DKC1 and XPC knockdown ES cells may be in part due to the reduced levels of OCT4 and NANOG, both of which have well-documented functions in antagonizing differentiation of extraembryonic lineages including the trophectoderm (Niwa et al., 2000; Hay et al., 2004; Hyslop et al., 2005; Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed gene expression changes and supported by citations to Niwa et al., 2000; Hay et al., 2004; Hyslop et al., 2005; Silva et al., 2009.

claim: Primary human adult fibroblasts (HFs) carrying pathogenic mutations in Dkc1 are refractory to cellular reprogramming.
source: Of note, recent studies showed that primary human adult fibroblasts (HFs) carrying pathogenic mutations in Dkc1 are refractory to cellular reprogramming (Agarwal et al., 2010; Batista et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Agarwal et al., 2010; Batista et al., 2011.

claim: MEFs display high levels of telomerase activity and long telomeres (>50 kb).
source: Unlike MEFs which display high levels of telomerase activity and long telomeres (>50 kb (Blasco et al., 1997)), HFs lack measurable TERT activity and have relatively short telomeres (10–15 kb (Harley et al., 1990)).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blasco et al., 1997.

claim: Human fibroblasts (HFs) lack measurable TERT activity and have relatively short telomeres (10–15 kb).
source: Unlike MEFs which display high levels of telomerase activity and long telomeres (>50 kb (Blasco et al., 1997)), HFs lack measurable TERT activity and have relatively short telomeres (10–15 kb (Harley et al., 1990)).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harley et al., 1990.

claim: Telomerase null MEFs can be propagated in culture for more than 200 cell divisions without loss of viability.
source: In fact, telomerase null MEFs can be propagated in culture for more than 200 cell divisions without loss of viability (Blasco et al., 1997), which make MEFs a potentially better cell culture system for studying telomerase-independent functions of DKC1 in reprogramming.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blasco et al., 1997.

claim: Ectopic expression of wild type DKC1 (or TERT) in a DC mutant fibroblast line (Dkc1 L37del) failed to rescue the reprogramming defect phenotype.
source: Consistent with this notion, it was shown that ectopic expression of wild type DKC1 (or TERT) in a DC mutant fibroblast line (Dkc1 L37del) failed to rescue the reprogramming defect phenotype (Agarwal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2010.

claim: DKC1 knockdown in MEFs resulted in a marked decrease (∼20–50-fold reduction) in the number of AP-positive iPS cell colonies.
source: We observed a marked decrease in the number of AP-positive iPS cell colonies (∼20–50-fold reduction) whether or not we plated the induced DKC1 knockdown MEFs directly onto gelatin coated plates (where the surrounding DKC1 knockdown MEFs refractory to reprogramming acted as feeder cells) or onto mitomycin-treated feeder cells (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Failure of DKC1-deficient MEFs to acquire pluripotency is likely a cell autonomous phenomenon.
source: This suggests that failure of DKC1-deficient MEFs to acquire pluripotency is likely a cell autonomous phenomenon.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reprogramming defects occur regardless of feeder cell conditions.

claim: The majority of both control and DKC1 knockdown cells down-regulated fibroblast-associated cell surface marker THY1 indicating a loss of MEF identity.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed that the majority of both control and DKC1 knockdown cells down-regulated fibroblast-associated cell surface marker THY1 indicating a loss of MEF identity (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Unlike control cells where many became SSEA1+ and gave rise to AP and NANOG-positive iPS cell colonies, most DKC1 knockdown cells do not.
source: However, unlike control cells where many of them became SSEA1+ and ultimately gave rise to AP and NANOG-positive iPS cell colonies, most DKC1 knockdown cells do not (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Depletion of DKC1 in MEFs blocked the reactivation of epithelial genes (Ecad and Epcam) without significantly perturbing the silencing of mesenchymal genes.
source: By contrast, depletion of DKC1 in MEFs blocked the reactivation of epithelial genes (Ecad and Epcam) without significantly perturbing the silencing of mesenchymal genes (Figure 7D), thus effectively uncoupling the otherwise tightly coordinated MET induced by OKSM (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: DKC1 could be required for reprogrammed MEFs to acquire an epithelial identity during the mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition.
source: These data taken together suggest that DKC1 could be required for reprogrammed MEFs to acquire an epithelial identity during the critically important mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the MET gene expression analysis in DKC1 knockdown MEFs.

claim: DKC1 depletion does not cause abrupt growth arrest of all MEFs but appears to selectively impair the proliferation of the faster cycling subpopulation.
source: We also note that DKC1 depletion does not cause abrupt growth arrest of all MEFs but appears to selectively impair the proliferation of the faster cycling subpopulation without affecting the rest of the slower-dividing MEFs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Essentially all of the reprogramming potential in OKSM-induced MEF cultures is confined to a small fraction (1–8%) of cells characterized by an ultrafast cell cycle.
source: These observations are also consistent with recent findings suggesting that essentially all of the reprogramming potential in OKSM-induced MEF cultures is confined to a small fraction (1–8%) of cells characterized by an ultrafast cell cycle (Smith et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2014.

claim: The fastest dividing population (CFSE-Lo) had undergone at least 4 more cell divisions than the bulk MEFs and gave rise to substantially more AP-positive iPS cell colonies than the slower-dividing populations.
source: The fastest dividing population (CFSE-Lo) had undergone at least 4 more cell divisions than the bulk MEFs and gave rise to substantially more AP-positive iPS cell colonies than the slower-dividing populations (Figure 8B; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: CFSE-Lo cells expressed the highest levels of Dkc1 reaching that of ES cells.
source: Strikingly, CFSE-Lo cells also expressed the highest levels of Dkc1 reaching that of ES cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: CFSE-Lo cells have lost their mesenchymal identity and initiated the transition into cells of epithelial origin.
source: These cells have lost their mesenchymal identity and initiated the transition into cells of epithelial origin (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The slower dividing populations expressed significantly lower levels of Dkc1 and failed to fully silence mesenchymal genes or robustly reactivate epithelial markers indicating a delayed or abortive MET.
source: By contrast, the slower dividing populations expressed significantly lower levels of Dkc1 and failed to fully silence mesenchymal genes or robustly reactivate epithelial markers indicating a delayed or abortive MET.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: Using MEFs carrying an integrated dox-inducible OKSM expression cassette, there was a similar preferential enrichment of Dkc1 in the fastest-dividing population (CFSE-Lo) despite uniform Oct4 expression levels among CFSE-Lo, Med, and Hi cells.
source: Importantly, using MEFs carrying an integrated dox-inducible OKSM expression cassette (Carey et al., 2010), we observed a similar preferential enrichment of Dkc1 in the fastest-dividing population (CFSE-Lo) despite uniform Oct4 expression levels among CFSE-Lo, Med, and Hi cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2,3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: An early onset of MET appears to be a defining property of ultrafast cycling cells wherein appropriately high levels of DKC1 are necessary and likely serve as an important gene-specific transcriptional coactivator.
source: Therefore, an early onset of MET appears to be a defining property of these ultrafast cycling cells wherein appropriately high levels of DKC1 are necessary and likely serve as an important gene-specific transcriptional coactivator.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between high Dkc1 expression, fast cell cycling, and early MET.

claim: The DKC1 complex has been shown to effect diverse cellular processes including internal ribosome entry site (IRES)-dependent translation.
source: Beyond its well-documented role in ribosome and telomerase biogenesis, the DKC1 complex has been shown to effect diverse cellular processes including internal ribosome entry site (IRES)-dependent translation (Yoon et al., 2006) and base excision of 5-hydroxymethyluridines in rRNA by uracil-DNA glycosylase 1 (SMUG1) (Jobert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoon et al., 2006.

claim: The DKC1 complex has been shown to effect base excision of 5-hydroxymethyluridines in rRNA by uracil-DNA glycosylase 1 (SMUG1).
source: Beyond its well-documented role in ribosome and telomerase biogenesis, the DKC1 complex has been shown to effect diverse cellular processes including internal ribosome entry site (IRES)-dependent translation (Yoon et al., 2006) and base excision of 5-hydroxymethyluridines in rRNA by uracil-DNA glycosylase 1 (SMUG1) (Jobert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jobert et al., 2013.

claim: The telomerase complex has been implicated in the regulation of MYC and WNT/β-catenin associated gene expression programs critical for stem cell function.
source: Interestingly, the telomerase complex itself has been implicated in the regulation of MYC and WNT/β-catenin associated gene expression programs critical for stem cell function (Choi et al., 2008; Park et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2008; Park et al., 2009.

claim: The reverse transcriptase TERT, but not its catalytic activity, was reported to be required for gene activation.
source: However, the reverse transcriptase TERT, but curiously not its catalytic activity, was reported to be required for gene activation (Choi et al., 2008), a finding that remains somewhat controversial in the telomerase field (Listerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2008; Listerman et al., 2014.

claim: The coactivator activity detected in the in vitro transcription assay is unlikely to be dependent on TERT because TERT or any other known components of the telomerase complex were not detected in the purified fractions by mass spectrometry.
source: It is, however, unlikely that the coactivator activity detected in our assay is dependent on TERT because we did not detect TERT or any other known components of the telomerase complex (Fu and Collins, 2007) in our purified fractions by mass spectrometry (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The DKC1 complex (free of any accessory factors) can be recruited to key pluripotency genes via a direct interaction with the XPC complex.
source: Instead, we favor the model whereby the DKC1 complex (free of any accessory factors) can be recruited to key pluripotency genes via a direct interaction with the XPC complex as we observed in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation results.

claim: The DKC1-XPC assembly is recruited to target gene promoters via activator–coactivator interactions with OCT4 and SOX2.
source: This DKC1-XPC assembly is, in turn, recruited to target gene promoters via activator–coactivator interactions with OCT4 and SOX2 (Fong et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fong et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2012.

claim: The Dkc1 gene itself is a target of OCT4 and NANOG.
source: Interestingly, the Dkc1 gene itself is also a target of OCT4 and NANOG (Agarwal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2010.

claim: Integrating Dkc1 into the core regulatory circuitry could further stabilize the autoregulatory loops established by OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG.
source: Integrating Dkc1 into the core regulatory circuitry could further stabilize the autoregulatory loops established by OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG that are postulated to confer stability to self-renewing ES cells without sacrificing their responsiveness to developmental cues during differentiation (Boyer et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Dkc1 is a target of OCT4 and NANOG and supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2006.

claim: As much as 90% of snoRNAs are embedded within introns of protein-coding genes in humans.
source: Because as much as 90% of snoRNAs are embedded within introns of protein-coding genes in humans (Dieci et al., 2009), their repertoire and relative abundance are directly coupled to the expression of their host genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dieci et al., 2009.

claim: The coactivator activity (and potentially specificity) of the DKC1 snoRNP can be coordinately regulated by cell type-dependent modulation of snoRNA composition.
source: Therefore, it is conceivable that the coactivator activity (and potentially specificity) of the DKC1 snoRNP can be coordinately regulated by cell type-dependent modulation of snoRNA composition.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression of snoRNAs and their effects on DKC1 activity.

claim: Many DC patients carrying mutations in the DKC1 complex live well into their teens and beyond, indicating that these mutations are hypomorphic and can be tolerated during embryogenesis.
source: Although targeted disruption of Dkc1 in mice is lethal (He et al., 2002), many DC patients carrying mutations in the DKC1 complex live well into their teens and beyond, indicating that these mutations are hypomorphic and can be tolerated during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2002 and general knowledge about DC patients.

claim: Amino acid residues in DKC1 critical for transcription are likely largely distinct from those mutated in DC patients.
source: These findings suggest that amino acid residues in DKC1 critical for transcription are likely largely distinct from those mutated in DC patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DC mutants are more active than wild-type in transcription assays.

claim: Acute depletion of DKC1 in mouse ES cells rapidly down-regulated key pluripotency genes well in advance of telomere attrition and cellular senescence.
source: Acute depletion of DKC1 in mouse ES cells rapidly down-regulated key pluripotency genes well in advance of telomere attrition and the ensuing cellular senescence that one would expect to occur (after >300 population doublings) due to compromised telomerase function (Niida et al., 1998; Mochizuki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Niida et al., 1998; Mochizuki et al., 2004.

claim: Defects in pluripotency gene expression and stem cell self-renewal upon DKC1 knockdown are at least in part due to compromised transcriptional activation rather than a sole consequence of telomerase deficiency.
source: Taken together with our ChIP results showing specific recruitment of the DKC1 complex to OCT4/SOX2 enhancers of core pluripotency genes in both mouse and human ES cells, as well as the strong dependence of OCT4/SOX2-activated transcription on the DKC1 complex in vitro, we suggest that defects in pluripotency gene expression and stem cell self-renewal upon DKC1 knockdown are at least in part due to compromised transcriptional activation rather than a sole consequence of telomerase deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of ChIP, in vitro transcription, and knockdown data.

claim: Reprogramming of DKC1-deficient MEFs by OKSM aborted at an early stage—during the mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET).
source: Our data, however, indicate that reprogramming of DKC1-deficient MEFs by OKSM aborted at a rather early stage—during the mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on MET gene expression analysis.

claim: DKC1 appears to be required for the proper induction of epithelial markers like Ecad critical for iPS cell generation.
source: Specifically, DKC1 appears to be required for the proper induction of epithelial markers like Ecad (also known as Cdh1) critical for iPS cell generation (Chen et al., 2010) even though key negative regulators of epithelial gene expression, Snail and Slug, were already repressed in DKC1 knockdown MEFs (Thiery et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010; Thiery et al., 2009.

claim: SOX2 (or KLF4) alone is sufficient to induce Ecad expression in MEFs.
source: Because SOX2 (or KLF4) alone is sufficient to induce Ecad expression in MEFs (Liu et al., 2013), and OKSM cotarget many MET genes early in the reprogramming process (Soufi et al., 2012), the DKC1 complex could cooperate with SOX2 and other reprogramming factors to activate an epithelial gene expression program.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013; Soufi et al., 2012.

claim: Restoring telomerase activity in DC patient-specific fibroblasts carrying a loss-of-function mutation in Dkc1 (L37del) by overexpressing TERT is insufficient to overcome the reprogramming defect.
source: It has also been reported that restoring telomerase activity in DC patient-specific fibroblasts carrying a loss-of-function mutation in Dkc1 (L37del) by overexpressing TERT (Wong and Collins, 2006) is insufficient to overcome the reprogramming defect associated with these cells (Agarwal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wong and Collins, 2006; Agarwal et al., 2010.

claim: L37del fibroblasts show normal rRNA pseudouridine content as well as rRNA processing kinetics.
source: Given that L37del fibroblasts show normal rRNA pseudouridine content as well as rRNA processing kinetics (Wong and Collins, 2006), these data taken together strongly suggests a telomerase and ribosome independent mechanism by which the DKC1 complex participates in somatic cell reprogramming.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wong and Collins, 2006.

claim: The DKC1 complex may function to promote the requisite MET during iPS cell generation by activating pro-epithelial genes consistent with its transcriptional coactivator function.
source: We propose that the DKC1 complex may function to promote the requisite MET during iPS cell generation by activating pro-epithelial genes consistent with its transcriptional coactivator function.
evidence: This is proposed based on the observed MET defects in DKC1 knockdown MEFs.

claim: Direct reprogramming of fibroblasts into iPS cells is a slow and presumably stochastic process.
source: Direct reprogramming of fibroblasts into iPS cells is a slow and presumably stochastic process (Yamanaka, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamanaka, 2009.

claim: Reprogramming is amenable to acceleration (and thereby enhanced efficiency) by manipulating pathways that promote cell division.
source: However, accumulating evidence suggests that it is nonetheless amenable to acceleration (and thereby enhanced efficiency) by manipulating pathways that promote cell division (Banito et al., 2009; Hanna et al., 2009; Hong et al., 2009; Utikal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banito et al., 2009; Hanna et al., 2009; Hong et al., 2009; Utikal et al., 2009.

claim: Highly proliferative cells competent for reprogramming are found to exist naturally or become primed by OKSM in a small subset of 'privileged' somatic cells.
source: These highly proliferative cells competent for reprogramming are also found to exist naturally or become primed by OKSM in a small subset of so called 'privileged' somatic cells within a largely homogeneous population that can proceed through reprogramming in a non-stochastic manner with shorter latency (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claim: A subpopulation of MEFs proliferating at a significantly faster rate is especially sensitive to DKC1 depletion.
source: Here we show that a subpopulation of MEFs proliferating at a significantly faster rate is especially sensitive to DKC1 depletion (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A small fraction of ultrafast cycling MEFs enriched for Dkc1 and depleted of mesenchymal signatures emerged upon OKSM expression.
source: Similarly, a small fraction of ultrafast cycling MEFs enriched for Dkc1 and depleted of mesenchymal signatures also emerged upon OKSM expression.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on CFSE labeling and sorting experiments.

claim: The intrinsic variable levels of DKC1 in regular MEFs, or the ability of some MEFs to upregulate Dkc1 to a critically high threshold level in response to ectopic expression of OKSM, could be a limiting factor in the acquisition of the rare privileged somatic cell state.
source: Therefore, the intrinsic variable levels of DKC1 in regular MEFs, or the ability of some MEFs to upregulate Dkc1 to a critically high threshold level in response to ectopic expression of OKSM, could be a limiting factor in the acquisition of this rare somatic cell state possibly by facilitating an early MET.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Dkc1 levels, cell cycling, and reprogramming efficiency.

claim: The DKC1 complex could be one of the cell-intrinsic determinants that impinges on somatic cells during reprogramming by coupling cellular proliferation to stem cell-specific transcription.
source: In summary, using an unbiased biochemical approach to probe the transcriptional regulation of the Nanog gene by OCT4 and SOX2, we uncovered an unanticipated transcriptional coactivator role of the DKC1 complex and a subset of its associated snoRNAs in ES and iPS cells. We surmise that the DKC1 complex could be one of the cell-intrinsic determinants that impinges on somatic cells during reprogramming by coupling cellular proliferation to stem cell-specific transcription.
evidence: This is the concluding statement summarizing the implications of the study.
